pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 13–14 years

- **Topic:** Motors & the Motor Effect

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3 Physics, 'Magnetism'):** 'the magnetic effect of a current, electromagnets, D.C. motors (principles only)'. [The full motor effect — force direction by the left-hand rule and F = BIL — sits at KS4 'Magnetism and electromagnetism'.]

- **Standards — US (NGSS, MS Forces & Interactions — MS-PS2-3):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-3] — the clarification explicitly names electric motors (e.g. the effect of the number/strength of magnets on the speed of an electric motor); DCI PS2.B. [The perpendicular force-direction geometry extends into HS-PS2.]

- **Operational details:** [No standalone operational prose preceded the markers in the source summary.]

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal-operational, age 13-14, the KS3→KS4 boundary). The hardest leap in the domain: a current-carrying conductor placed in an external magnetic field experiences a force that is PERPENDICULAR to BOTH the current and the field (a genuinely 3D relationship), and reversing either the current or the field reverses the force — the basis of the electric motor and the loudspeaker. At KS3 this stays at 'predict the direction the wire is pushed and that reversing current or field reverses it' (D.C. motors, principles only); the left-hand rule and quantitative F = BIL belong to KS4. Honest stance (IOP/Oak): predict and observe the motion; explaining the underlying field-interaction mechanism is beyond this level — don't substitute a hand-wavy wrong model.
bestPractices: Sequence predict → observe → reconcile, but only AFTER pupils have enough theory — research shows real apparatus can otherwise trigger 'gut-feeling' reversion to force-along-the-field thinking.
Let pupils discover the direction-dependence empirically by reversing the current and reversing the magnets BEFORE the left-hand rule is introduced as a summary.
Explicitly SEPARATE the two rules pupils conflate: 'the field produced by a current' versus 'the force on a current in a field'.
Pre-empt the electrostatics import — directly confront 'opposites attract' reasoning applied to current-carrying wires; magnetism is not electrostatics.

Teach the perpendicular 3D relationship deliberately (force ⊥ both current and field; maximum when the wire is perpendicular to the field, zero when along it) using a physical three-axis prop or hand.

Use the classic demo — a stiff copper wire or foil strip between slab (Magnadur) magnets on an iron yoke — then connect the same force on the two sides of a coil to the turning motor and to the loudspeaker cone; be honest that the deeper 'why' is left for later.
keyRepresentations: A wire between magnet poles with three mutually-perpendicular arrows: current, field (N→S) and force
Side-by-side reverse-current and reverse-field cases showing the force flip
A physical three-axis hand/prop modelling force ⊥ (current, field)
A coil in a field → turning effect → motor with a split ring; a loudspeaker cone driven by the force
The left-hand rule shown as a SUMMARY introduced after the empirical direction-dependence (KS4)
commonMisconceptions: Importing 'opposites attract' from electrostatics to current-carrying wires (Singh).
Expecting the wire to be pushed TOWARD a pole (along the field) rather than perpendicular to it (Singh).
Believing the force and the field point in the SAME direction — a gut-feeling error, strongest when shown real apparatus (Singh).
Mixing up the 'field from a current' rule and the 'force on a current' rule (Singh).
Treating the multi-step reasoning (field, then force) as a single guess, and memorising outcomes (e.g. 'opposite currents repel') without being able to reason them (Singh).
Thinking the explanation of HOW the two fields interact is required at this level — it is deliberately out of scope (Oak/IOP).

learn.summary: For ages 13–14 (KS3→KS4 boundary), learners build the motor effect: a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force that is perpendicular to BOTH the current and the field, and reversing either the current or the field reverses the force. The lead activity is a predict → observe → reconcile cycle on a motor-effect bench (physical demo or live simulation) with independent reverse-current and reverse-field controls, so each cause is isolated and the direction pattern (later named the left-hand rule) is discovered rather than handed down. Complementary activities attack the non-intuitive 3D perpendicularity, drill direction prediction, and label motor/loudspeaker parts. At KS3 the goal is to predict and observe the motion and connect it to the motor and loudspeaker; the quantitative F = BIL and a full field-interaction explanation belong to KS4 and later.

activities.title: Motor-effect bench: predict, run, reconcile
feedback: If a learner predicts the wire is pulled toward a pole: run it so they see the sideways kick (impossible for simple attraction), and name the force as perpendicular to both current and field.
If they expect 'nothing changes' when the current reverses: isolate the reverse-current control and let them watch the kick flip — this is the direct test that it is not ordinary magnetic attraction.
If they predict a flip when BOTH inputs are reversed: have them reason that two reversals cancel, then demonstrate the wire jumping the original way.
Confirm the discovered pattern before introducing the left-hand rule, so the rule reads as their finding, not an imposed trick.
activities.rationale: Independent reverse-current and reverse-field controls isolate each cause of the force's direction, and letting pupils discover the direction-dependence empirically before the left-hand rule is introduced as a summary addresses documented misconceptions (attraction-to-a-pole, force-along-the-field). Predicting before switching surfaces gut-feeling reasoning so it can be confronted. Efficacy of this proposed sequence is research-informed but not independently validated here.
sourceClaims: There is a force on a current-carrying wire at right angles to both current and field; maximum when perpendicular, zero when the wire lies along the field; reversing current or field reverses the force; demonstrate with slab magnets on a yoke and a stiff wire/foil, reversing current and magnets before introducing the left-hand rule; honestly admit the field-interaction explanation is beyond the syllabus.

Documented student misconceptions: importing 'opposites attract' from electrostatics to current-carrying wires; expecting deflection toward a pole rather than perpendicular; treating force and field as parallel (gut-feeling, worse with real apparatus); mixing up the field-from-current and force-on-current rules; fragile multi-step reasoning and memorised-without-reasoning outcomes.
KS3 'Magnetism' statutory content: the magnetic effect of a current, electromagnets, D.C. motors (principles only).
learnerActions: View a straight wire hanging between a north and a south pole, seen end-on (use real slab/Magnadur magnets on an iron yoke with a stiff copper wire or foil strip, or a live end-on simulation).
BEFORE switching on, predict which way the wire will move and say why.

Run it and observe: from rest the wire kicks SIDEWAYS, perpendicular to both the current and the field — either out of the gap or deeper into it, depending on the current and field directions — not toward either pole.
Use an independent reverse-current control: flip only the current and observe the kick reverse.
Use an independent reverse-field control: flip only the magnets and observe the kick reverse again.
Flip BOTH current and field together and predict first — observe that the kick returns to the original direction.
After several (current, field) → force rounds, state the pattern you found in your own words; then meet the left-hand rule as a summary of that pattern.

'Roll the wire up' into a coil and observe that, because the current flows in opposite directions along the two sides, they feel forces in opposite directions, which together turn the coil (a motor; a split ring reverses the current every half turn so it keeps turning the same way); see how a changing current drives a cone in a loudspeaker.
activities.intendedInsight: The force on a current-carrying wire is perpendicular to both the current and the field; reversing either input reverses the force while reversing both restores it; a wire that is free and initially at rest therefore starts to move in the direction of that force, and the same force turns a motor coil and moves a loudspeaker cone.

activities.title: Orienting the three axes: force ⊥ both current and field
feedback: If a learner draws the force parallel to the current or to the field, point back to the three-axis prop and have them physically set the third perpendicular axis.
Reinforce the max-when-perpendicular / zero-when-parallel cases by having them rotate the wire relative to the field and report when the force shrinks to nothing.
activities.rationale: The central hurdle is the non-intuitive 3D geometry that students struggle to visualise; a reorientable three-axis model lets learners see the perpendicularity directly. This is a scaffold for the perpendicularity insight and is best used after the 2D direction-dependence is secure. A 3D model offers a different view from the 2D bench; neither is claimed to be universally necessary.
sourceClaims: There is a force on a current-carrying wire at right angles to both current and field; maximum when perpendicular, zero when the wire lies along the field; reversing current or field reverses the force; demonstrate with slab magnets on a yoke and a stiff wire/foil, reversing current and magnets before introducing the left-hand rule; honestly admit the field-interaction explanation is beyond the syllabus.

Documented student misconceptions: importing 'opposites attract' from electrostatics to current-carrying wires; expecting deflection toward a pole rather than perpendicular; treating force and field as parallel (gut-feeling, worse with real apparatus); mixing up the field-from-current and force-on-current rules; fragile multi-step reasoning and memorised-without-reasoning outcomes.
learnerActions: Work with three mutually-perpendicular axes representing current, field (N→S), and force — using a physical three-axis hand/prop, or a 3D model you can reorient and view from any angle.
Set the current axis and the field axis in space, then identify the force on the third, perpendicular axis.
Rotate the viewpoint to confirm the force stays perpendicular to both regardless of how you look at it.
Explore the special cases: the force is maximum when the wire is perpendicular to the field, and zero when the wire lies along the field.
activities.intendedInsight: The force is always perpendicular to both the current and the field; when the wire is at right angles to the field (where the force is largest), current, field and force are all mutually perpendicular — a genuinely three-dimensional relationship that a single flattened view can hide.

activities.title: Predict the force direction and separate the two rules
feedback: If a learner gives the force along the field toward a pole and says reversing the current makes no difference, treat it as the attraction misconception: return to the bench's reverse-current test.
If they recite a memorised outcome (e.g. 'opposite currents repel') without being able to reason it, have them rebuild the field-then-force steps rather than quoting the result.
If they confuse the two rules, ask explicitly 'is this the field a current makes, or the force a current feels?' before they answer.
activities.rationale: Prediction, reverse-input, and step-sequencing tasks drill the direction-dependence and force the two commonly-conflated rules apart. Note this is recognition/short-answer practice: it can check and strengthen reasoning but does not by itself elicit the independent construction that the hands-on bench does.
sourceClaims: Documented student misconceptions: importing 'opposites attract' from electrostatics to current-carrying wires; expecting deflection toward a pole rather than perpendicular; treating force and field as parallel (gut-feeling, worse with real apparatus); mixing up the field-from-current and force-on-current rules; fragile multi-step reasoning and memorised-without-reasoning outcomes.
learnerActions: Given a current direction and a field direction, predict which way the force pushes the wire.
Answer reverse-current and reverse-field tasks: state how the force direction changes when only one input flips, and when both flip.
Sequence the reasoning: first identify the field, THEN apply the force rule — do not treat it as a single guess.
Match a motor and a loudspeaker to the motor-effect principle they rely on.
Distinguish 'the field produced by a current' from 'the force on a current in a field' when a question could invite either.
activities.intendedInsight: Direction of the force follows reliably from the current and field via multi-step reasoning, and the 'field from a current' rule is not the same as the 'force on a current' rule.

activities.title: Label the arrows, the motor and the loudspeaker
feedback: Confirm correct arrow labels against the left-hand-rule card.
If a learner cannot say why the coil keeps turning, prompt them toward the split ring's role in maintaining rotation past half a turn.
activities.rationale: A labelling summary consolidates vocabulary and the motor/loudspeaker application. It is a companion to the bench, not a replacement: a static labelled image shows the arrangement but cannot animate the kick or the reversals, so direction-dependence should be discovered first on the bench and only reviewed here.
sourceClaims: KS3 'Magnetism' statutory content: the magnetic effect of a current, electromagnets, D.C. motors (principles only).
learnerActions: Label the three arrows on a wire-between-poles diagram: current, field (N→S), and force.
Label the parts of a D.C. motor (coil, magnets, split ring) and a loudspeaker (coil, magnet, cone).
Use a left-hand-rule reference card to check the arrow directions.
Explain in a sentence how the force on the coil's two sides produces rotation, and how a changing current moves the cone in and out.
activities.intendedInsight: The same perpendicular force appears in a diagram, a motor and a loudspeaker; the parts and arrow directions can be named and connected to the principle.

constraints: KS3 scope: predict the push direction and that reversing current or field reverses it, and grasp the motor/loudspeaker principle. The left-hand rule is formally KS4 content; at this boundary it may be previewed only as a summary of the pattern pupils have already found. The quantitative F = BIL belongs to KS4.
Be honest that explaining HOW the two magnetic fields interact to produce the force is deliberately out of scope at this level — do not substitute a hand-wavy or wrong mechanism.

Sequence predict → observe → reconcile only AFTER pupils have enough background that a force is expected; real apparatus shown too early can trigger gut-feeling reversion to force-along-the-field thinking.
Directly confront the imported 'opposites attract' electrostatics reasoning: the force on current-carrying wires is not electrostatic attraction.
The labelling activity is a static summary scaffold: a static image can show the arrangement but cannot animate the reversals, so it should follow the hands-on bench rather than lead.

The 3D-axis activity is a scaffold scoped to the perpendicularity insight; use it after the 2D direction-dependence is secure. A 2D view and a 3D model give different experiences; neither is asserted to be the only way to learn.
The prediction/reverse-input practice is recognition-style and checks reasoning; it does not substitute for independent hands-on construction of the effect.

Describe the wire's motion in terms of the force: a free wire initially at rest begins to accelerate and move in the force direction; do not state that a single force's direction is generally 'the direction of travel' in other contexts.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two cited sources were marked unverified in the original row (IOP Spark/Oak on the motor effect, and Singh arXiv:1701.01523 on misconceptions); their claims should be re-checked before being relied upon as evidence.

Self-audit of the physics: reversing only current OR only field reverses the force, while reversing BOTH restores the original direction (two reversals cancel); the force is perpendicular to both current and field, not along either; from rest the free wire accelerates in the force direction. Retained as the core correct model.

The original framing that the conversation/persona artefact is categorically 'poor' and that a flattened 2D view 'cannot' address the 3D misconception was softened to narrow affordances: dialogue is ill-suited to building a manipulated direction relationship, and a static 2D view hides (rather than is universally incapable of teaching) the perpendicularity. No comparative efficacy claim beyond the sources is asserted.

The labelling activity's sourceClaims were reduced to the KS3 D.C.-motors statutory claim; the MS-PS2-3 'number/strength of magnets affects motor speed' claim was removed because it matches the topic but not that activity's teaching principle. MS-PS2-3 remains relevant context for the domain but is not built into an activity here.

Independent re-audit found the physics, initial conditions, causal logic, source-principle matches, and media affordance claims internally consistent; no new critical learner-facing errors were identified.

assess.poeTask: Set up a wire between the poles of a magnet so it can swing freely, and pass a current — it kicks. Ask students to predict which way it kicks and what happens when you reverse ONLY the current, and WHY, before switching. Predicting 'nothing changes, it's just attracted' versus 'it kicks the opposite way' reveals whether they see a current-in-a-field force or plain magnetic attraction.
probeDeeper: If you reversed the current AND swapped the magnet's poles at the same time, which way would the wire jump? Why?
In an electric motor, why does the coil keep turning the same way instead of jamming after half a turn?
A loudspeaker uses this effect — what is the current doing to make the cone move in and out?
Is the wire being 'attracted' to the magnet? What test would show it isn't?
assess.correctAnswer: The force is at right angles to BOTH the current and the field (not along either) — it pushes the wire perpendicular to the field lines and to the current direction. Reversing only the current reverses the direction of the force, so the wire jumps the other way. (Reversing the field alone also reverses it; reversing both leaves it unchanged.)

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The wire is just attracted to the magnet, like iron — the force pulls it toward a pole.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that reversing the current flips the wire's jump — impossible for simple attraction; establish that the force is perpendicular to both current and field.
errorPatterns.distractor: The wire is pulled toward the nearest magnet pole, the way iron is attracted.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the force direction ALONG the field toward a pole and says reversing the current makes no difference.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The force points along the current (or along the field lines).'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use Fleming's left-hand rule and a clear three-direction demo; stress the three directions are mutually perpendicular.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws the force parallel to the current or to the field, not perpendicular to both.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Reversing BOTH the current and the magnet's poles reverses the force.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reason it through (two reversals cancel) and demonstrate — the wire jumps the same way as at the start.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts a flip when both inputs are reversed at once.

responseLevels.gap: Treats it as ordinary attraction — force toward a pole, reversing the current does nothing; or puts the force along the current/field.
responseLevels.full: Explains the force is perpendicular to both current and field, predicts the direction change for reversing current, field, or both, and applies the effect to a motor (with the split-ring maintaining rotation) and to a loudspeaker.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the wire feels a force and that reversing the current flips it, but can't state the perpendicular relationship, or gets the 'both reversed' case wrong — the reverse rules are recited, not reasoned.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A wire carrying a current sits between the poles of a magnet, and the wire suddenly jumps — it feels a force. Which way does the force push the wire, compared with the current and the magnetic field — and what happens to that push if I reverse ONLY the current?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student who understands the motor effect says the force is PERPENDICULAR to both current and field and that reversing one input flips it. A student who thinks it's ordinary magnetic attraction says the wire is 'pulled toward' a pole (force along the field) and that reversing the current does nothing (a magnet 'just attracts metal'). The direction relationship and the reverse-one-input test are the discriminators.
